title: If the Lord wills (James 4:11–17)
hook: you are a mist that appears for a little while

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise with two sides, draw near to God, and your line was draw near.

Open your calendar app. Look at next month, laid out in neat colored blocks: the trip, the deadline, the dentist, the dinner. It looks so certain on the screen. Now think back to a year ago. How much of what you planned then happened the way you planned it? James turns to people making plans like that: traders off to a city for a year to buy and sell. And he sounds like he's reading over their shoulder.

First a quick word against speaking evil of one another: there is one judge, he says, so who are you to judge your neighbor? Then the business plan. In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain." Very specific, and very confident. Then James says: "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." A vapor. The breath you see on a cold morning. The steam off a cup of coffee. The mist on a field at dawn that's gone by nine. It's real, and then it isn't. James doesn't say, so don't plan. He gives better words for planning: "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that." Make the plan. Hold it with an open hand. The phrase passed into Christian speech. Some still write the Latin letters D.V., Deo volente, God willing, at the bottom of a letter about future plans. Muslims say something close, in sha' Allah, if God wills, and Jews say im yirtzeh Hashem. It's a shared human humility about tomorrow. And the passage ends with a line that turns it around: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin." If life is a vapor, the good you know you could do is for today. Not someday.

Picture your plans for the rest of today and tomorrow, each one written on a little card, held in an open hand instead of a fist, and notice which one you're gripping hardest. Breathe out slowly and watch the breath disappear, the way James's vapor does. If you pray, you can offer your plans to God.
Vapor. James's picture for a life that's here today and gone tomorrow: the breath you see on a cold morning, real, and then gone.
Your line: a little while. Plans in an open hand. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians add "God willing" or "Lord willing" when speaking of future plans, and some still write D.V., for Deo volente, at the end of a letter or a notice of meetings.
